claims.sentence: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection in any part of the urinary system, which includes the kidneys, the tubes that carry urine, the bladder and the urethra.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection - NHS is described as a type of UTI; UTI page covers bladder/urinary symptoms (cystitis). Whole-system wording is clearly equivalent.

claims.sentence: Cystitis is the name for an infection of the bladder.
claims.evidence: Cystitis - NHS page returned but no excerpt stated the definition; plain undisputed fact.

claims.sentence: The NHS describes UTIs as common, and many of them are cystitis.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text says UTIs are common or that many are cystitis.

claims.sentence: The NHS lists pain or burning when passing urine, needing to pass urine more often or more urgently than usual, and cloudy urine.
claims.evidence: UTI page: burning when passing urine, needing to go more often (including at night), cloudy or bloody urine. 'More urgently' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists burning or pain when passing urine, needing to pass urine more often (including at night), and cloudy urine.

claims.sentence: Cystitis can also bring lower tummy pain.
claims.evidence: UTI page: lower tummy or back pain among symptoms.

claims.sentence: A kidney infection is more serious.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection can become serious without treatment; needs prompt antibiotics.

claims.sentence: Symptoms that point towards it include a high temperature, pain in the back or side under the ribs, feeling shivery or unwell, and blood in the urine.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection page: very high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery; pain in lower tummy or back just under the ribs; blood in pee. ('Unwell' is general.)

claims.sentence: Older or frail people may show confusion or drowsiness rather than typical urinary symptoms.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection page: in older people it may cause confusion. Drowsiness, frailty and 'rather than urinary symptoms' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: In older people, a kidney infection may cause confusion.

claims.sentence: UTIs happen when bacteria, usually from the gut, get into the urinary tract.
claims.evidence: Most UTIs start when bacteria from the bowel travel up the urethra; E. coli most common (summary blended, attribution moderate).

claims.sentence: Pregnancy, using spermicide with contraception and not drinking enough fluids are among the things the NHS links with a higher chance of getting one.
claims.evidence: Pregnancy, spermicide-coated condoms/diaphragms and low fluid intake listed as risk factors (summary blended; the 'NHS links' attribution is moderate).

claims.sentence: People who use a urinary catheter, or who have a weakened immune system, are also at higher risk.
claims.evidence: Catheter and weakened immunity listed as risk factors; NHS urgent-help list includes both.

claims.sentence: Mild cases can settle without antibiotics.
claims.evidence: UTI page: antibiotics are not always needed; most cases can be eased at home; GPs may wait a couple of days. 'Settle' not stated.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says antibiotics are not always needed, and many cases can be eased at home.

claims.sentence: The NHS says drinking plenty of fluids and taking a painkiller such as paracetamol can ease symptoms, and that there is no good evidence to support cranberry products.
claims.evidence: Fluids and paracetamol supported. Cranberry: no evidence that cranberry products or sachets help ease symptoms or treat an infection already started; some people take them to prevent UTIs and they may help. Blanket 'no good evidence' overstates (source is NHS 111 Wales / Notts leaflet, not the English page).
claims.newSentence: The NHS says paracetamol and drinking plenty of fluids can ease symptoms, and NHS guidance says there is no evidence that cranberry products help ease symptoms once an infection has started.

claims.sentence: A GP or pharmacist may offer antibiotics, usually a short course for cystitis.
claims.evidence: GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics; pharmacists advise on treatment and whether to see a GP (some pharmacies may supply antibiotics). 'Usually' short course for cystitis not firmly attributed; Mersey Care says most women get 3 days.
claims.newSentence: A pharmacist can advise on treatment and whether you need a GP, and a GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics.

claims.sentence: Sometimes the clinician may provide a prescription to be used only if symptoms do not improve.
claims.evidence: Only 'GPs may suggest waiting a couple of days' retrieved; no back-up prescription statement.

claims.sentence: A urine sample can be tested, although this is not always needed.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text about urine testing.

claims.sentence: Kidney infections are usually treated with a longer course of antibiotics, and some people need care in hospital.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection page: most need prompt antibiotics; vulnerable people (long-term condition, pregnant) may be admitted for antibiotics by drip. 'Longer course' not stated for kidney infection.
claims.newSentence: Most kidney infections need prompt treatment with antibiotics, and some people, such as those who are pregnant or have a long-term health condition, may be treated in hospital.

claims.sentence: The NHS advises contacting a GP or NHS 111 the same day for blood in the urine, pain in the back or side, a very high or low temperature, vomiting, or not having passed urine all day.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection page urgent GP or NHS 111 list: very high temperature or hot/cold/shivery, temperature below 36C, pain in lower tummy or back under ribs, blood in pee, feeling or being sick, no pee all day.

claims.sentence: The same applies to anyone who is pregnant, uses a catheter or has a weakened immune system.
claims.evidence: UTI page: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if pregnant, use a catheter, have a weakened immune system or keep getting UTIs.

claims.sentence: A GP appointment is the route when symptoms have not cleared within a few days, after antibiotics, or when UTIs keep coming back.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection page: see a GP if urinary symptoms have not improved after a few days; UTI page: keep getting UTIs means urgent GP/111. 'After antibiotics' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP if urinary symptoms have not improved after a few days, or if UTIs keep coming back.

claims.sentence: Confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking can be a sign of a serious infection, and the route is 999 or A&E.
claims.evidence: NHS: being confused, drowsy or having difficulty speaking means call 999 or go to A&E now; do not drive yourself.

claims.sentence: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection anywhere in the urinary system, and cystitis is a UTI in the bladder.
claims.evidence: As c01/c02.

claims.sentence: Common symptoms are pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often or urgently, and cloudy urine.
claims.evidence: 'Urgently' not retrieved (see c04).
claims.newSentence: Common symptoms are pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often, and cloudy urine.

claims.sentence: Fever, pain in the back or side below the ribs, or blood in the urine can point to a more serious infection.
claims.evidence: Kidney infection urgent-help list (very high temperature, back pain under ribs, blood in pee).

claims.sentence: Antibiotics are used for many UTIs, but the NHS says they are not always needed, and mild cases can settle on their own.
claims.evidence: Antibiotics not always needed and most cases can be eased at home retrieved; 'settle on their own' not.
claims.newSentence: Antibiotics can treat UTIs, but the NHS says they are not always needed and many cases can be eased at home.

claims.sentence: Urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP is advised for symptoms such as blood in the urine, back pain or a high temperature.
claims.evidence: Urgent GP/NHS 111 list as in c18. Suggest also naming 999 for confusion, drowsiness or trouble speaking.

claims.sentence: A urinary tract infection (UTI) can affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys; cystitis is a UTI of the bladder, and many cases are treated with antibiotics.
claims.evidence: 'Many cases are treated with antibiotics' not backed; NHS stresses antibiotics are not always needed.
claims.newSentence: A urinary tract infection (UTI) can affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys; cystitis is a UTI of the bladder, and antibiotics are not always needed.

notes: Only 4 searches used. Retrieval returned summaries, not page text; several items (cranberry, pharmacist, bowel bacteria, risk factors) come from blended summaries and NHS 111 Wales/trust leaflets rather than the English NHS pages. Cystitis - NHS page returned no excerpt, so cystitis definition is classed textbook. Cranberry sentence should preferably be reconfirmed against nhs.uk wording before publication.
